h: Nerves, timings and a Halifax afternoon
p: First time on an auto-belay? Here's the honest truth: the climbing bit is easy, it's the letting go that gets people. Most first-timers cling on at the top for a good few seconds, convinced the line won't catch them. It always does. A good trick is to let go from just a metre or two up on your first wall, feel the gentle drop, then go higher every time after that. By the end of the session you'll be launching yourself off without a second thought.

Timing-wise, think of it as a couple of hours door to door. Turn up a bit early so the paperwork, harness fitting and briefing don't eat into your climbing time, and expect your arms to feel it more than your legs. Have something light to eat beforehand rather than a full fry-up, and bring a water bottle, because you will get warm. There's normally a minimum age and some rules about adults supervising little ones, so check the details for your crew when you book.

Got time to spare after? Dean Clough, the huge old carpet mill complex turned arts and business hub, is a fascinating place to wander, with galleries and spots for a coffee. Halifax Minster is right in the middle of town and well worth a peek inside, and Bankfield Museum has plenty of local history. If you fancy a change of scene altogether, Hebden Bridge is just up the Calder Valley for canal-side strolls and independent shops.
